methodology: Evidence recall measures recovery of exact, labeled source passages; document recall measures source-page recovery. MRR measures the rank of the first relevant passage. nDCG rewards first recovery of each gold evidence item. Query embeddings are requested once per question without a cache, and the same measured embedding latency is charged to both semantic and hybrid search. BM25 requires no API. All strategies use the same top-5 and two-chunks-per-document cap. Bootstrap intervals resample questions 2,000 times with a fixed seed. Answer evaluation uses cold query embeddings, serial generation requests, exact-quote validation, and a separate source-conditioned judge.
limitations: Small, author-curated benchmark: 32 answerable questions and 8 abstention cases. It is not a production workload or an independent SOTA benchmark.
Questions and gold labels were created by the project author with AI assistance. The holdout split was frozen before the initial run, but is not blinded or independently adjudicated.
Gold passage anchors are intentionally strict and incomplete. A different valid passage may be scored as a miss. Document recall is reported separately.
Exact quotation verifies provenance, not entailment. The separate LLM judge is a fallible proxy and may share biases with the answer model; read its per-claim verdicts.
Latency is from one machine and one serial run, not a load test or an SLA. External API latency, caches, and service conditions affect it.
This corpus covers Kubernetes 1.35 core documentation. It cannot observe a cluster, confirm its root cause, or cover every operator, cloud provider, or newer version.

result.title: CPU throttling at limit

claims.text: Yes—slowing down at a CPU limit is expected behavior. Kubernetes says CPU limits are enforced by throttling, and a container may be restricted at its limit rather than terminated.

citations.quote:
Both `cpu` and `memory` limits are applied by the kubelet (and
container runtime),
and are ultimately enforced by the kernel.

`cpu` limits are enforced by CPU throttling. When a container approaches
its `cpu` limit, the kernel will restrict access to the CPU corresponding to the
container's limit.

A container might or might not be allowed to exceed its CPU limit for extended periods of time.
However, container runtimes don't terminate Pods or containers for excessive CPU usage.

claims.text: By contrast, Kubernetes documents memory limit exceedance as a condition that can lead to termination or OOMKilled behavior, which is different from CPU limits.

citations.quote:
`memory` limits are enforced by the kernel with out of memory (OOM) kills. When
a container uses more than its `memory` limit, the kernel may terminate it.

If a Container allocates more memory than
its limit, the Container becomes a candidate for termination. If the Container continues to
consume memory beyond its limit, the Container is terminated.
